Issued at 539 AM CDT Sun Aug 2 2026

Positively-tilted upper level ridge extends from the Desert 
Southwest through the Northern Plains early this morning. A 
"cold" front/surface trough is moving from central into eastern 
Montana, attendant to a Canadian surface cyclone whose parent 
upper low is crossing the Canadian Rockies. Low level jet 
induced warm air advection has generated some isolated sprinkles
or light rain showers in northern parts of the state early this
morning, and this activity may continue into the early 
afternoon while sliding eastward. The front will enter western 
North Dakota later this morning and reach central North Dakota 
this afternoon before it begins to stall as the Canadian low 
occludes. The thermal ridge axis should mostly align with the 
frontal interface, which gives high confidence in the hottest 
temperatures at or slightly above 100 degrees in south central 
North Dakota this afternoon. Heat indices should be similar to 
air temperatures in this part of the state as dewpoints fall 
into the 50s or perhaps 40s. A Heat Advisory has been issued 
for Morton, Grant, Sioux, Burleigh, and Emmons Counties from 
noon to 8 PM CDT. High temperatures will be cooler with 
increasing distance from the Heat Advisory, mostly in the 90s 
but with mid to upper 80s far northwest. Windy conditions are 
anticipated both ahead of and behind the front, but may 
actually be lighter along the frontal interface. Already seeing
breezy southerly winds early this morning, which should 
increase to 20-30 mph with gusts near 40 mph in central North 
Dakota this afternoon. Behind the cold front, northwest winds 
are expected to increase to around 20 mph with gusts to 30 mph 
through early afternoon, but then decrease later in the 
afternoon as mean boundary layer winds become lighter. The 
combination of windy conditions and very low humidity will 
produce near-critical to critical fire weather conditions in 
the western half of the state today. See the fire section below
for details.

The occluded Canadian low will spin across Saskatchewan late 
tonight, pushing mid level height falls into the Northern 
Plains and turning flow aloft southwesterly. Underneath, the 
surface front is forecast to stall from northeast to south 
central North Dakota. The increase in synoptic scale forcing, 
including an increasing low level jet on the leeward side of 
the surface trough, could initiate scattered showers and 
thunderstorms over parts of the state late tonight into Monday 
morning. While MUCAPE could increase above 1000 J/kg and 
effective bulk shear for the most-unstable elevated parcels 
could increase above 40 kts, most CAM guidance is pessimistic 
that the maximum CAPE/shear parameter space will be realized. A
few UH tracks do begin to show up in the Devils Lake Basin and 
James River Valley by around 6 AM CDT Monday morning, but this 
is not universal among all CAMs. We will continue to advertise 
a strong to marginal severe storm risk tonight into Monday 
morning, with baseline severe hazards of quarter size hail and 
wind gusts near 60 mph.

During the day Monday, a separate shortwave ejecting from the 
American side of the Northern Rockies will join forces with the 
Canadian occluded low and push a secondary but much stronger 
cold front into the Northern Plains. High temperatures could 
still reach the 80s in south central and eastern North Dakota, 
but the northwest corner of the state may struggle to rise 
above 70! Windy conditions will also continue on Monday, out of 
the north to northwest around 25 to 30 mph with gusts to near 
40 mph. Despite the cooler temperatures, humidity will still 
fall low enough to prolong fire weather concerns south and west 
of the Missouri River. Please refer to the fire section below 
for further details. The other concern for Monday is the 
eastward progression of the lead surface trough and trailing 
shortwave, which will determine whether mid to late-day 
thunderstorms develop in our forecast area. CAMs show a mixture 
of potential outcomes, ranging from no storms after the morning 
(e.g., the 06Z HRRR) to scattered strong to severe storms in the
eastern half of the state late Monday afternoon and evening 
(e.g., the 06Z NAMnest). It is difficult to put too much weight 
into any specific outcome given the potential for the midday 
environment to be modified by morning convection. We will 
therefore tie the severe risk on Monday in with that of 
tonight/Monday morning for messaging purposes.

Forecast confidence is high that surface high pressure will 
build into the region on Tuesday under an upper level longwave 
trough. This should bring below normal temperatures to all, 
with highs on Tuesday in the 70s and lows around 45 to 50 both
